title: Fairness
body:
[[Starvation]]

A scheduling policy is fair when no process is systematically disadvantaged: everyone
runnable gets the CPU reasonably often, and everyone waiting for a lock eventually gets it.
Its failure is [[Starvation]].

Fairness is a *policy* goal, not a correctness property, which is why the course states the
correctness version separately as [[Bounded Waiting]]. Bounded waiting is the formal claim
(there is an upper bound on your time in the entry section); fairness is the informal one
(the bound is also reasonable).

The reason it is a trade rather than a free win: the most efficient schedule is almost
never the fairest one. Running the shortest job first maximises throughput and starves long
jobs. Strict [[Process Priority]] gets urgent work done first and starves everything else.
Shorter time slices spread the CPU more evenly and spend more of it on
[[Context Switching|context switches]]. Every mechanism that buys fairness (aging, round
robin, [[FIFO]] [[Wait Queue|wait queues]]) costs something measurable.
